CHAPTER I

One day something happened to Fionn, the son of Uail; that is, he
departed from the world of men, and was set wandering in great distress
of mind through Faery. He had days and nights there and adventures
there, and was able to bring back the memory of these.

That, by itself, is wonderful, for there are few people who remember
that they have been to Faery or aught of all that happened to them in
that state.

In truth we do not go to Faery, we become Faery, and in the beating of a
pulse we may live for a year or a thousand years. But when we return
the memory is quickly clouded, and we seem to have had a dream or seen a
vision, although we have verily been in Faery.

It was wonderful, then, that Fionn should have remembered all that
happened to him in that wide-spun moment, but in this tale there is yet
more to marvel at; for not only did Fionn go to Faery, but the great
army which he had marshalled to Ben Edair [The Hill of Howth] were
translated also, and neither he nor they were aware that they had
departed from the world until they came back to it.

Fourteen battles, seven of the reserve and seven of the regular Fianna,
had been taken by the Chief on a great march and manoeuvre. When they
reached Ben Edair it was decided to pitch camp so that the troops
might rest in view of the warlike plan which Fionn had imagined for the
morrow. The camp was chosen, and each squadron and company of the host
were lodged into an appropriate place, so there was no overcrowding and
no halt or interruption of the march; for where a company halted that
was its place of rest, and in that place it hindered no other company,
and was at its own ease.

When this was accomplished the leaders of battalions gathered on a
level, grassy plateau overlooking the sea, where a consultation began
as to the next day’s manoeuvres, and during this discussion they looked
often on the wide water that lay wrinkling and twinkling below them.

A roomy ship under great press of sall was bearing on Ben Edair from the
east.

Now and again, in a lull of the discussion, a champion would look and
remark on the hurrying vessel; and it may have been during one of these
moments that the adventure happened to Fionn and the Fianna.

“I wonder where that ship comes from?” said Cona’n idly.

But no person could surmise anything about it beyond that it was a
vessel well equipped for war.

As the ship drew by the shore the watchers observed a tall man swing
from the side by means of his spear shafts, and in a little while this
gentleman was announced to Fionn, and was brought into his presence.

A sturdy, bellicose, forthright personage he was indeed. He was equipped
in a wonderful solidity of armour, with a hard, carven helmet on
his head, a splendid red-bossed shield swinging on his shoulder, a
wide-grooved, straight sword clashing along his thigh. On his shoulders
under the shield he carried a splendid scarlet mantle; over his breast
was a great brooch of burnt gold, and in his fist he gripped a pair of
thick-shafted, unburnished spears.

Fionn and the champions looked on this gentleman, and they admired
exceedingly his bearing and equipment.

“Of what blood are you, young gentleman?” Fionn demanded, “and from
which of the four corners of the world do you come?”

“My name is Cael of the Iron,” the stranger answered, “and I am son to
the King of Thessaly.”

“What errand has brought you here?”

“I do not go on errands,” the man replied sternly, “but on the affairs
that please me.”

“Be it so. What is the pleasing affair which brings you to this land?”

“Since I left my own country I have not gone from a land or an island
until it paid tribute to me and acknowledged my lordship.”

“And you have come to this realm,” cried Fionn, doubting his ears.

“For tribute and sovereignty,” growled that other, and he struck the
haft of his spear violently on the ground.

“By my hand,” said Cona’n, “we have never heard of a warrior, however
great, but his peer was found in Ireland, and the funeral songs of all
such have been chanted by the women of this land.”

“By my hand and word,” said the harsh stranger, “your talk makes me
think of a small boy or of an idiot.”

“Take heed, sir,” said Fionn, “for the champions and great dragons of
the Gael are standing by you, and around us there are fourteen battles
of the Fianna of Ireland.”

“If all the Fianna who have died in the last seven years were added to
all that are now here,” the stranger asserted, “I would treat all of
these and those grievously, and would curtail their limbs and their
lives.”

“It is no small boast,” Cona’n murmured, staring at him.

“It is no boast at all,” said Cael, “and, to show my quality and
standing, I will propose a deed to you.”

“Give out your deed,” Fionn commanded.

“Thus,” said Cael with cold savagery. “If you can find a man among your
fourteen battalions who can outrun or outwrestle or outfight me, I will
take myself off to my own country, and will trouble you no more.”

And so harshly did he speak, and with such a belligerent eye did he
stare, that dismay began to seize on the champions, and even Fionn felt
that his breath had halted.

“It is spoken like a hero,” he admitted after a moment, “and if you
cannot be matched on those terms it will not be from a dearth of
applicants.”

“In running alone,” Fionn continued thoughtfully, “we have a notable
champion, Caelte mac Rona’n.”

“This son of Rona’n will not long be notable,” the stranger asserted.

“He can outstrip the red deer,” said Cona’n.

“He can outrun the wind,” cried Fionn.

“He will not be asked to outrun the red deer or the wind,” the stranger
sneered. “He will be asked to outrun me,” he thundered. “Produce this
runner, and we shall discover if he keeps as great heart in his feet as
he has made you think.”

“He is not with us,” Cona’n lamented.

“These notable warriors are never with us when the call is made,” said
the grim stranger.

“By my hand,” cried Fionn, “he shall be here in no great time, for I
will fetch him myself.”

“Be it so,” said Cael. “And during my absence,” Fionn continued, “I
leave this as a compact, that you make friends with the Fianna here
present, and that you observe all the conditions and ceremonies of
friendship.”

Cael agreed to that.

“I will not hurt any of these people until you return,” he said.

Fionn then set out towards Tara of the Kings, for he thought Caelte mac
Romin would surely be there; “and if he is not there,” said the champion
to himself, “then I shall find him at Cesh Corran of the Fianna.”

CHAPTER II

He had not gone a great distance from Ben Edair when he came to
an intricate, gloomy wood, where the trees grew so thickly and the
undergrowth was such a sprout and tangle that one could scarcely pass
through it. He remembered that a path had once been hacked through the
wood, and he sought for this. It was a deeply scooped, hollow way, and
it ran or wriggled through the entire length of the wood.

Into this gloomy drain Fionn descended and made progress, but when he
had penetrated deeply in the dank forest he heard a sound of thumping
and squelching footsteps, and he saw coming towards him a horrible,
evil-visaged being; a wild, monstrous, yellow-skinned, big-boned giant,
dressed in nothing but an ill-made, mud-plastered, drab-coloured coat,
which swaggled and clapped against the calves of his big bare legs. On
his stamping feet there were great brogues of boots that were shaped
like, but were bigger than, a boat, and each time he put a foot down it
squashed and squirted a barrelful of mud from the sunk road.

Fionn had never seen the like of this vast person, and he stood gazing
on him, lost in a stare of astonishment.

The great man saluted him.

“All alone, Fionn?” he cried. “How does it happen that not one Fenian
of the Fianna is at the side of his captain?” At this inquiry Fionn got
back his wits.

“That is too long a story and it is too intricate and pressing to be
told, also I have no time to spare now.”

“Yet tell it now,” the monstrous man insisted.

Fionn, thus pressed, told of the coming of Cael of the Iron, of the
challenge the latter had issued, and that he, Fionn, was off to Tara of
the Kings to find Caelte mac Rona’n.

“I know that foreigner well,” the big man commented.

“Is he the champion he makes himself out to be?” Fionn inquired.

“He can do twice as much as he said he would do,” the monster replied.

“He won’t outrun Caelte mac Rona’n,” Fionn asserted. The big man jeered.

“Say that he won’t outrun a hedgehog, dear heart. This Cael will end the
course by the time your Caelte begins to think of starting.”

“Then,” said Fionn, “I no longer know where to turn, or how to protect
the honour of Ireland.”

“I know how to do these things,” the other man commented with a slow nod
of the head.

“If you do,” Fionn pleaded, “tell it to me upon your honour.”

“I will do that,” the man replied.

“Do not look any further for the rusty-kneed, slow-trotting son of
Rona’n,” he continued, “but ask me to run your race, and, by this hand,
I will be first at the post.”

At this the Chief began to laugh.

“My good friend, you have work enough to carry the two tons of mud that
are plastered on each of your coat-tails, to say nothing of your weighty
boots.”

“By my hand,” the man cried, “there is no person in Ireland but myself
can win that race. I claim a chance.”

Fionn agreed then. “Be it so,” said he. “And now, tell me your name?”

“I am known as the Carl of the Drab Coat.”

“All names are names,” Fionn responded, “and that also is a name.”

They returned then to Ben Edair.

CHAPTER III

When they came among the host the men of Ireland gathered about the vast
stranger; and there were some who hid their faces in their mantles so
that they should not be seen to laugh, and there were some who rolled
along the ground in merriment, and there were others who could only hold
their mouths open and crook their knees and hang their arms and stare
dumbfoundedly upon the stranger, as though they were utterly dazed.

Cael of the Iron came also on the scene, and he examined the stranger
with close and particular attention.

“What in the name of the devil is this thing?” he asked of Fionn.

“Dear heart,” said Fionn, “this is the champion I am putting against you
in the race.”

Cael of the Iron grew purple in the face, and he almost swallowed his
tongue through wrath.

“Until the end of eternity,” he roared, “and until the very last moment
of doom I will not move one foot in a race with this greasy, big-hoofed,
ill-assembled resemblance of a beggarman.”

But at this the Carl burst into a roar of laughter, so that the eardrums
of the warriors present almost burst inside of their heads.

“Be reassured, my darling, I am no beggarman, and my quality is not more
gross than is the blood of the most delicate prince in this assembly.
You will not evade your challenge in that way, my love, and you shall
run with me or you shall run to your ship with me behind you. What
length of course do you propose, dear heart?”

“I never run less than sixty miles,” Cael replied sullenly.

“It is a small run,” said the Carl, “but it will do. From this place
to the Hill of the Rushes, Slieve Luachra of Munster, is exactly sixty
miles. Will that suit you?”

“I don’t care how it is done,” Cael answered.

“Then,” said the Carl, “we may go off to Slieve Luachra now, and in the
morning we can start our race there to here.”

“Let it be done that way,” said Cael.

These two set out then for Munster, and as the sun was setting they
reached Slieve Luachra and prepared to spend the night there.

CHAPTER IV

“Cael, my pulse,” said the Carl, “we had better build a house or a hut
to pass the night in.”

“I’Il build nothing,” Cael replied, looking on the Carl with great
disfavour.

“No!”

“I won’t build house or hut for the sake of passing one night here, for
I hope never to see this place again.”

“I’Il build a house myself,” said the Carl, “and the man who does not
help in the building can stay outside of the house.”

The Carl stumped to a near-by wood, and he never rested until he had
felled and tied together twenty-four couples of big timber. He thrust
these under one arm and under the other he tucked a bundle of rushes for
his bed, and with that one load he rushed up a house, well thatched and
snug, and with the timber that remained over he made a bonfire on the
floor of the house.

His companion sat at a distance regarding the work with rage and
aversion.

“Now Cael, my darling,” said the Carl, “if you are a man help me to look
for something to eat, for there is game here.”

“Help yourself,” roared Cael, “for all that I want is not to be near
you.”

“The tooth that does not help gets no helping,” the other replied.

In a short time the Carl returned with a wild boar which he had run
down. He cooked the beast over his bonfire and ate one half of it,
leaving the other half for his breakfast. Then he lay down on the
rushes, and in two turns he fell asleep.

But Cael lay out on the side of the hill, and if he went to sleep that
night he slept fasting. It was he, however, who awakened the Carl in the
morning.

“Get up, beggarman, if you are going to run against me.”

The Carl rubbed his eyes.

“I never get up until I have had my fill of sleep, and there is another
hour of it due to me. But if you are in a hurry, my delight, you can
start running now with a blessing. I will trot on your track when I
waken up.”

Cael began to race then, and he was glad of the start, for his
antagonist made so little account of him that he did not know what to
expect when the Carl would begin to run.

“Yet,” said Cael to himself, “with an hour’s start the beggarman will
have to move his bones if he wants to catch on me,” and he settled down
to a good, pelting race.

CHAPTER V

At the end of an hour the Carl awoke. He ate the second half of the
boar, and he tied the unpicked bones in the tail of his coat. Then with
a great rattling of the boar’s bones he started.

It is hard to tell how he ran or at what speed he ran, but he went
forward in great two-legged jumps, and at times he moved in
immense one-legged, mud-spattering hops, and at times again, with
wide-stretched, far-flung, terrible-tramping, space-destroying legs he
ran.

He left the swallows behind as if they were asleep. He caught up on
a red deer, jumped over it, and left it standing. The wind was always
behind him, for he outran it every time; and he caught up in jumps and
bounces on Cael of the Iron, although Cael was running well, with
his fists up and his head back and his two legs flying in and out so
vigorously that you could not see them because of that speedy movement.

Trotting by the side of Cael, the Carl thrust a hand into the tail of
his coat and pulled out a fistfull of red bones.

“Here, my heart, is a meaty bone,” said he, “for you fasted all night,
poor friend, and if you pick a bit off the bone your stomach will get a
rest.”

“Keep your filth, beggarman,” the other replied, “for I would rather be
hanged than gnaw on a bone that you have browsed.”

“Why don’t you run, my pulse?” said the Carl earnestly; “why don’t you
try to win the race?”

Cael then began to move his limbs as if they were the wings of a fly,
or the fins of a little fish, or as if they were the six legs of a
terrified spider.

“I am running,” he gasped.

“But try and run like this,” the Carl admonished, and he gave a
wriggling bound and a sudden outstretching and scurrying of shanks, and
he disappeared from Cael’s sight in one wild spatter of big boots.

Despair fell on Cael of the Iron, but he had a great heart. “I will run
until I burst,” he shrieked, “and when I burst, may I burst to a great
distance, and may I trip that beggar-man up with my burstings and make
him break his leg.”

He settled then to a determined, savage, implacable trot. He caught up
on the Carl at last, for the latter had stopped to eat blackberries from
the bushes on the road, and when he drew nigh, Cael began to jeer and
sneer angrily at the Carl.

“Who lost the tails of his coat?” he roared.

“Don’t ask riddles of a man that’s eating blackberries,” the Carl
rebuked him.

“The dog without a tall and the coat without a tail,” cried Cael.

“I give it up,” the Carl mumbled.

“It’s yourself, beggarman,” jeered Cael.

“I am myself,” the Carl gurgled through a mouthful of blackberries,
“and as I am myself, how can it be myself? That is a silly riddle,” he
burbled.

“Look at your coat, tub of grease?”

The Carl did so.

“My faith,” said he, “where are the two tails of my coat?” “I could
smell one of them and it wrapped around a little tree thirty miles
back,” said Cael, “and the other one was dishonouring a bush ten miles
behind that.”

“It is bad luck to be separated from the tails of your own coat,” the
Carl grumbled. “I’ll have to go back for them. Wait here, beloved, and
eat blackberries until I come back, and we’ll both start fair.”

“Not half a second will I wait,” Cael replied, and he began to run
towards Ben Edair as a lover runs to his maiden or as a bee flies to his
hive.

“I haven’t had half my share of blackberries either,” the Carl lamented
as he started to run backwards for his coat-tails.

He ran determinedly on that backward journey, and as the path he had
travelled was beaten out as if it had been trampled by an hundred bulls
yoked neck to neck, he was able to find the two bushes and the two
coat-tails. He sewed them on his coat.

Then he sprang up, and he took to a fit and a vortex and an exasperation
of running for which no description may be found. The thumping of his
big boots grew as con-tinuous as the pattering of hailstones on a
roof, and the wind of his passage blew trees down. The beasts that were
ranging beside his path dropped dead from concussion, and the steam that
snored from his nose blew birds into bits and made great lumps of cloud
fall out of the sky.

He again caught up on Cael, who was running with his head down and his
toes up.

“If you won’t try to run, my treasure,” said the Carl, “you will never
get your tribute.”

And with that he incensed and exploded himself into an eye-blinding,
continuous, waggle and complexity of boots that left Cael behind him in
a flash.

“I will run until I burst,” sobbed Cael, and he screwed agitation and
despair into his legs until he hummed and buzzed like a blue-bottle on a
window.

Five miles from Ben Edair the Carl stopped, for he had again come among
blackberries.

He ate of these until he was no more than a sack of juice, and when
he heard the humming and buzzing of Cael of the Iron he mourned and
lamented that he could not wait to eat his fill He took off his coat,
stuffed it full of blackberries, swung it on his shoulders, and went
bounding stoutly and nimbly for Ben Edair.

CHAPTER VI

It would be hard to tell of the terror that was in Fionn’s breast and
in the hearts of the Fianna while they attended the conclusion of that
race.

They discussed it unendingly, and at some moment of the day a man
upbraided Fionn because he had not found Caelte the son of Rona’n as had
been agreed on.

“There is no one can run like Caelte,” one man averred.

“He covers the ground,” said another.

“He is light as a feather.”

“Swift as a stag.” “Lunged like a bull.”

“Legged like a wolf.”

“He runs!”

These things were said to Fionn, and Fionn said these things to himself.

With every passing minute a drop of lead thumped down into every heart,
and a pang of despair stabbed up to every brain.

“Go,” said Fionn to a hawk-eyed man, “go to the top of this hill and
watch for the coming of the racers.”

And he sent lithe men with him so that they might run back in endless
succession with the news.

The messengers began to run through his tent at minute intervals calling
“nothing,” “nothing,” “nothing,” as they paused and darted away.

And the words, “nothing, nothing, nothing,” began to drowse into the
brains of every person present.

“What can we hope from that Carl?” a champion demanded savagely.

“Nothing,” cried a messenger who stood and sped.

“A clump!” cried a champion.

“A hog!” said another.

“A flat-footed.”

“Little-wlnded.”

“Big-bellied.”

“Lazy-boned.”

“Pork!”

“Did you think, Fionn, that a whale could swim on land, or what did you
imagine that lump could do?”

“Nothing,” cried a messenger, and was sped as he spoke.

Rage began to gnaw in Fionn’s soul, and a red haze danced and flickered
before his eyes. His hands began to twitch and a desire crept over him
to seize on champions by the neck, and to shake and worry and rage among
them like a wild dog raging among sheep.

He looked on one, and yet he seemed to look on all at once.

“Be silent,” he growled. “Let each man be silent as a dead man.”

And he sat forward, seeing all, seeing none, with his mouth drooping
open, and such a wildness and bristle lowering from that great glum brow
that the champions shivered as though already in the chill of death, and
were silent.

He rose and stalked to the tent-door.

“Where to, O Fionn?” said a champion humbly.

“To the hill-top,” said Fionn, and he stalked on.

They followed him, whispering among themselves, keeping their eyes on
the ground as they climbed.

CHAPTER VII

“What do you see?” Fionn demanded of the watcher.

“Nothing,” that man replied.

“Look again,” said Fionn.

The eagle-eyed man lifted a face, thin and sharp as though it had been
carven on the wind, and he stared forward with an immobile intentness.

“What do you see?” said Fionn.

“Nothing,” the man replied.

“I will look myself,” said Fionn, and his great brow bent forward and
gloomed afar.

The watcher stood beside, staring with his tense face and unwinking,
lidless eye.

“What can you see, O Fionn?” said the watcher.

“I can see nothing,” said Fionn, and he projected again his grim, gaunt
forehead. For it seemed as if the watcher stared with his whole face,
aye, and with his hands; but Fionn brooded weightedly on distance with
his puckered and crannied brow.

They looked again.

“What can you see?” said Fionn.

“I see nothing,” said the watcher.

“I do not know if I see or if I surmise, but something moves,” said
Fionn. “There is a trample,” he said.

The watcher became then an eye, a rigidity, an intense out-thrusting and
ransacking of thin-spun distance. At last he spoke.

“There is a dust,” he said.

And at that the champions gazed also, straining hungrily afar, until
their eyes became filled with a blue darkness and they could no longer
see even the things that were close to them.

“I,” cried Cona’n triumphantly, “I see a dust.”

“And I,” cried another.

“And I.”

“I see a man,” said the eagle-eyed watcher.

And again they stared, until their straining eyes grew dim with tears
and winks, and they saw trees that stood up and sat down, and fields
that wobbled and spun round and round in a giddily swirling world.

“There is a man,” Cona’n roared.

“A man there is,” cried another.

“And he is carrying a man on his back,” said the watcher.

“It is Cael of the Iron carrying the Carl on his back,” he groaned.

“The great pork!” a man gritted.

“The no-good!” sobbed another.

“The lean-hearted.”

“Thick-thighed.”

“Ramshackle.”

“Muddle-headed.”

“Hog!” screamed a champion.

And he beat his fists angrily against a tree.

But the eagle-eyed watcher watched until his eyes narrowed and became
pin-points, and he ceased to be a man and became an optic.

“Wait,” he breathed, “wait until I screw into one other inch of sight.”

And they waited, looking no longer on that scarcely perceptible speck in
the distance, but straining upon the eye of the watcher as though they
would penetrate it and look through it.

“It is the Carl,” he said, “carrying something on his back, and behind
him again there is a dust.”

“Are you sure?” said Fionn in a voice that rumbled and vibrated like
thunder.

“It is the Carl,” said the watcher, “and the dust behind him is Cael of
the Iron trying to catch him up.”

Then the Fianna gave a roar of exultation, and each man seized his
neighbour and kissed him on both cheeks; and they gripped hands about
Fionn, and they danced round and round in a great circle, roaring with
laughter and relief, in the ecstasy which only comes where grisly fear
has been and whence that bony jowl has taken itself away.

CHAPTER VIII

The Carl of the Drab Coat came bumping and stumping and clumping into
the camp, and was surrounded by a multitude that adored him and hailed
him with tears.

“Meal!” he bawled, “meal for the love of the stars!”

And he bawled, “Meal, meal!” until he bawled everybody into silence.

Fionn addressed him.

“What for the meal, dear heart?”

“For the inside of my mouth,” said the Carl, “for the recesses and
crannies and deep-down profundities of my stomach. Meal, meal!” he
lamented.

Meal was brought.

The Carl put his coat on the ground, opened it carefully, and revealed
a store of blackberries, squashed, crushed, mangled, democratic,
ill-looking.

“The meal!” he groaned, “the meal!”

It was given to him.

“What of the race, my pulse?” said Fionn.

“Wait, wait,” cried the Carl. “I die, I die for meal and blackberries.”

Into the centre of the mess of blackberries he discharged a barrel of
meal, and be mixed the two up and through, and round and down, until
the pile of white-black, red-brown slibber-slobber reached up to his
shoulders. Then he commenced to paw and impel and project and cram the
mixture into his mouth, and between each mouthful he sighed a contented
sigh, and during every mouthful he gurgled an oozy gurgle.

But while Fionn and the Fianna stared like lost minds upon the Carl,
there came a sound of buzzing, as if a hornet or a queen of the wasps or
a savage, steep-winged griffin was hovering about them, and looking away
they saw Cael of the Iron charging on them with a monstrous extension
and scurry of his legs. He had a sword in his hand, and there was
nothing in his face but redness and ferocity.

Fear fell llke night around the Fianna, and they stood with slack knees
and hanging hands waiting for death. But the Carl lifted a pawful of his
oozy slop and discharged this at Cael with such a smash that the man’s
head spun off his shoulders and hopped along the ground. The Carl then
picked up the head and threw it at the body with such aim and force
that the neck part of the head jammed into the neck part of the body and
stuck there, as good a head as ever, you would have said, but that it
bad got twisted the wrong way round. The Carl then lashed his opponent
hand and foot.

“Now, dear heart, do you still claim tribute and lordship of Ireland?”
 said he.

“Let me go home,” groaned Cael, “I want to go home.”

“Swear by the sun and moon, if I let you go home, that you will send to
Fionn, yearly and every year, the rent of the land of Thessaly.”

“I swear that,” said Cael, “and I would swear anything to get home.”

The Carl lifted him then and put him sitting into his ship. Then he
raised his big boot and gave the boat a kick that drove it seven leagues
out into the sea, and that was how the adventure of Cael of the Iron
finished.

“Who are you, sir?” said Fionn to the Carl.

But before answering the Carl’s shape changed into one of splendour and
delight.

“I am ruler of the Shi’ of Rath Cruachan,” he said.

Then Fionn mac Uail made a feast and a banquet for the jovial god, and
with that the tale is ended of the King of Thessaly’s son and the Carl
of the Drab Coat.
paragraphs: CHAPTER I

One day something happened to Fionn, the son of Uail; that is, he departed from the world of men, and was set wandering in great distress of mind through Faery. He had days and nights there and adventures there, and was able to bring back the memory of these.
That, by itself, is wonderful, for there are few people who remember that they have been to Faery or aught of all that happened to them in that state.

In truth we do not go to Faery, we become Faery, and in the beating of a pulse we may live for a year or a thousand years. But when we return the memory is quickly clouded, and we seem to have had a dream or seen a vision, although we have verily been in Faery.

It was wonderful, then, that Fionn should have remembered all that happened to him in that wide-spun moment, but in this tale there is yet more to marvel at; for not only did Fionn go to Faery, but the great army which he had marshalled to Ben Edair [The Hill of Howth] were translated also, and neither he nor they were aware that they had departed from the world until they came back to it.

Fourteen battles, seven of the reserve and seven of the regular Fianna, had been taken by the Chief on a great march and manoeuvre. When they reached Ben Edair it was decided to pitch camp so that the troops might rest in view of the warlike plan which Fionn had imagined for the morrow. The camp was chosen, and each squadron and company of the host were lodged into an appropriate place, so there was no overcrowding and no halt or interruption of the march; for where a company halted that was its place of rest, and in that place it hindered no other company, and was at its own ease.

When this was accomplished the leaders of battalions gathered on a level, grassy plateau overlooking the sea, where a consultation began as to the next day’s manoeuvres, and during this discussion they looked often on the wide water that lay wrinkling and twinkling below them.
A roomy ship under great press of sall was bearing on Ben Edair from the east.

Now and again, in a lull of the discussion, a champion would look and remark on the hurrying vessel; and it may have been during one of these moments that the adventure happened to Fionn and the Fianna.
“I wonder where that ship comes from?” said Cona’n idly.
But no person could surmise anything about it beyond that it was a vessel well equipped for war.

As the ship drew by the shore the watchers observed a tall man swing from the side by means of his spear shafts, and in a little while this gentleman was announced to Fionn, and was brought into his presence.

A sturdy, bellicose, forthright personage he was indeed. He was equipped in a wonderful solidity of armour, with a hard, carven helmet on his head, a splendid red-bossed shield swinging on his shoulder, a wide-grooved, straight sword clashing along his thigh. On his shoulders under the shield he carried a splendid scarlet mantle; over his breast was a great brooch of burnt gold, and in his fist he gripped a pair of thick-shafted, unburnished spears.
Fionn and the champions looked on this gentleman, and they admired exceedingly his bearing and equipment.
“Of what blood are you, young gentleman?” Fionn demanded, “and from which of the four corners of the world do you come?”
“My name is Cael of the Iron,” the stranger answered, “and I am son to the King of Thessaly.”
“What errand has brought you here?”
“I do not go on errands,” the man replied sternly, “but on the affairs that please me.”
“Be it so. What is the pleasing affair which brings you to this land?”
“Since I left my own country I have not gone from a land or an island until it paid tribute to me and acknowledged my lordship.”
“And you have come to this realm,” cried Fionn, doubting his ears.
“For tribute and sovereignty,” growled that other, and he struck the haft of his spear violently on the ground.
“By my hand,” said Cona’n, “we have never heard of a warrior, however great, but his peer was found in Ireland, and the funeral songs of all such have been chanted by the women of this land.”
“By my hand and word,” said the harsh stranger, “your talk makes me think of a small boy or of an idiot.”
“Take heed, sir,” said Fionn, “for the champions and great dragons of the Gael are standing by you, and around us there are fourteen battles of the Fianna of Ireland.”

“If all the Fianna who have died in the last seven years were added to all that are now here,” the stranger asserted, “I would treat all of these and those grievously, and would curtail their limbs and their lives.”
“It is no small boast,” Cona’n murmured, staring at him.
“It is no boast at all,” said Cael, “and, to show my quality and standing, I will propose a deed to you.”
“Give out your deed,” Fionn commanded.

“Thus,” said Cael with cold savagery. “If you can find a man among your fourteen battalions who can outrun or outwrestle or outfight me, I will take myself off to my own country, and will trouble you no more.”
And so harshly did he speak, and with such a belligerent eye did he stare, that dismay began to seize on the champions, and even Fionn felt that his breath had halted.
“It is spoken like a hero,” he admitted after a moment, “and if you cannot be matched on those terms it will not be from a dearth of applicants.”
“In running alone,” Fionn continued thoughtfully, “we have a notable champion, Caelte mac Rona’n.”
“This son of Rona’n will not long be notable,” the stranger asserted.
“He can outstrip the red deer,” said Cona’n.
“He can outrun the wind,” cried Fionn.

“He will not be asked to outrun the red deer or the wind,” the stranger sneered. “He will be asked to outrun me,” he thundered. “Produce this runner, and we shall discover if he keeps as great heart in his feet as he has made you think.”
“He is not with us,” Cona’n lamented.
“These notable warriors are never with us when the call is made,” said the grim stranger.
“By my hand,” cried Fionn, “he shall be here in no great time, for I will fetch him myself.”

“Be it so,” said Cael. “And during my absence,” Fionn continued, “I leave this as a compact, that you make friends with the Fianna here present, and that you observe all the conditions and ceremonies of friendship.”
Cael agreed to that.
“I will not hurt any of these people until you return,” he said.

Fionn then set out towards Tara of the Kings, for he thought Caelte mac Romin would surely be there; “and if he is not there,” said the champion to himself, “then I shall find him at Cesh Corran of the Fianna.”
CHAPTER II

He had not gone a great distance from Ben Edair when he came to an intricate, gloomy wood, where the trees grew so thickly and the undergrowth was such a sprout and tangle that one could scarcely pass through it. He remembered that a path had once been hacked through the wood, and he sought for this. It was a deeply scooped, hollow way, and it ran or wriggled through the entire length of the wood.

Into this gloomy drain Fionn descended and made progress, but when he had penetrated deeply in the dank forest he heard a sound of thumping and squelching footsteps, and he saw coming towards him a horrible, evil-visaged being; a wild, monstrous, yellow-skinned, big-boned giant, dressed in nothing but an ill-made, mud-plastered, drab-coloured coat, which swaggled and clapped against the calves of his big bare legs. On his stamping feet there were great brogues of boots that were shaped like, but were bigger than, a boat, and each time he put a foot down it squashed and squirted a barrelful of mud from the sunk road.
Fionn had never seen the like of this vast person, and he stood gazing on him, lost in a stare of astonishment.
The great man saluted him.
“All alone, Fionn?” he cried. “How does it happen that not one Fenian of the Fianna is at the side of his captain?” At this inquiry Fionn got back his wits.
“That is too long a story and it is too intricate and pressing to be told, also I have no time to spare now.”
“Yet tell it now,” the monstrous man insisted.
Fionn, thus pressed, told of the coming of Cael of the Iron, of the challenge the latter had issued, and that he, Fionn, was off to Tara of the Kings to find Caelte mac Rona’n.
“I know that foreigner well,” the big man commented.
“Is he the champion he makes himself out to be?” Fionn inquired.
“He can do twice as much as he said he would do,” the monster replied.
“He won’t outrun Caelte mac Rona’n,” Fionn asserted. The big man jeered.
“Say that he won’t outrun a hedgehog, dear heart. This Cael will end the course by the time your Caelte begins to think of starting.”
“Then,” said Fionn, “I no longer know where to turn, or how to protect the honour of Ireland.”
“I know how to do these things,” the other man commented with a slow nod of the head.
“If you do,” Fionn pleaded, “tell it to me upon your honour.”
“I will do that,” the man replied.
“Do not look any further for the rusty-kneed, slow-trotting son of Rona’n,” he continued, “but ask me to run your race, and, by this hand, I will be first at the post.”
At this the Chief began to laugh.
“My good friend, you have work enough to carry the two tons of mud that are plastered on each of your coat-tails, to say nothing of your weighty boots.”
“By my hand,” the man cried, “there is no person in Ireland but myself can win that race. I claim a chance.”
Fionn agreed then. “Be it so,” said he. “And now, tell me your name?”
“I am known as the Carl of the Drab Coat.”
“All names are names,” Fionn responded, “and that also is a name.”
They returned then to Ben Edair.
CHAPTER III

When they came among the host the men of Ireland gathered about the vast stranger; and there were some who hid their faces in their mantles so that they should not be seen to laugh, and there were some who rolled along the ground in merriment, and there were others who could only hold their mouths open and crook their knees and hang their arms and stare dumbfoundedly upon the stranger, as though they were utterly dazed.
Cael of the Iron came also on the scene, and he examined the stranger with close and particular attention.
“What in the name of the devil is this thing?” he asked of Fionn.
“Dear heart,” said Fionn, “this is the champion I am putting against you in the race.”
Cael of the Iron grew purple in the face, and he almost swallowed his tongue through wrath.
“Until the end of eternity,” he roared, “and until the very last moment of doom I will not move one foot in a race with this greasy, big-hoofed, ill-assembled resemblance of a beggarman.”
But at this the Carl burst into a roar of laughter, so that the eardrums of the warriors present almost burst inside of their heads.

“Be reassured, my darling, I am no beggarman, and my quality is not more gross than is the blood of the most delicate prince in this assembly. You will not evade your challenge in that way, my love, and you shall run with me or you shall run to your ship with me behind you. What length of course do you propose, dear heart?”
“I never run less than sixty miles,” Cael replied sullenly.
“It is a small run,” said the Carl, “but it will do. From this place to the Hill of the Rushes, Slieve Luachra of Munster, is exactly sixty miles. Will that suit you?”
“I don’t care how it is done,” Cael answered.
“Then,” said the Carl, “we may go off to Slieve Luachra now, and in the morning we can start our race there to here.”
“Let it be done that way,” said Cael.
These two set out then for Munster, and as the sun was setting they reached Slieve Luachra and prepared to spend the night there.
CHAPTER IV
“Cael, my pulse,” said the Carl, “we had better build a house or a hut to pass the night in.”
“I’Il build nothing,” Cael replied, looking on the Carl with great disfavour.
“No!”
“I won’t build house or hut for the sake of passing one night here, for I hope never to see this place again.”
“I’Il build a house myself,” said the Carl, “and the man who does not help in the building can stay outside of the house.”

The Carl stumped to a near-by wood, and he never rested until he had felled and tied together twenty-four couples of big timber. He thrust these under one arm and under the other he tucked a bundle of rushes for his bed, and with that one load he rushed up a house, well thatched and snug, and with the timber that remained over he made a bonfire on the floor of the house.
His companion sat at a distance regarding the work with rage and aversion.
“Now Cael, my darling,” said the Carl, “if you are a man help me to look for something to eat, for there is game here.”
“Help yourself,” roared Cael, “for all that I want is not to be near you.”
“The tooth that does not help gets no helping,” the other replied.

In a short time the Carl returned with a wild boar which he had run down. He cooked the beast over his bonfire and ate one half of it, leaving the other half for his breakfast. Then he lay down on the rushes, and in two turns he fell asleep.
But Cael lay out on the side of the hill, and if he went to sleep that night he slept fasting. It was he, however, who awakened the Carl in the morning.
“Get up, beggarman, if you are going to run against me.”
The Carl rubbed his eyes.

“I never get up until I have had my fill of sleep, and there is another hour of it due to me. But if you are in a hurry, my delight, you can start running now with a blessing. I will trot on your track when I waken up.”
Cael began to race then, and he was glad of the start, for his antagonist made so little account of him that he did not know what to expect when the Carl would begin to run.
“Yet,” said Cael to himself, “with an hour’s start the beggarman will have to move his bones if he wants to catch on me,” and he settled down to a good, pelting race.
CHAPTER V
At the end of an hour the Carl awoke. He ate the second half of the boar, and he tied the unpicked bones in the tail of his coat. Then with a great rattling of the boar’s bones he started.

It is hard to tell how he ran or at what speed he ran, but he went forward in great two-legged jumps, and at times he moved in immense one-legged, mud-spattering hops, and at times again, with wide-stretched, far-flung, terrible-tramping, space-destroying legs he ran.

He left the swallows behind as if they were asleep. He caught up on a red deer, jumped over it, and left it standing. The wind was always behind him, for he outran it every time; and he caught up in jumps and bounces on Cael of the Iron, although Cael was running well, with his fists up and his head back and his two legs flying in and out so vigorously that you could not see them because of that speedy movement.
Trotting by the side of Cael, the Carl thrust a hand into the tail of his coat and pulled out a fistfull of red bones.
“Here, my heart, is a meaty bone,” said he, “for you fasted all night, poor friend, and if you pick a bit off the bone your stomach will get a rest.”
“Keep your filth, beggarman,” the other replied, “for I would rather be hanged than gnaw on a bone that you have browsed.”
“Why don’t you run, my pulse?” said the Carl earnestly; “why don’t you try to win the race?”
Cael then began to move his limbs as if they were the wings of a fly, or the fins of a little fish, or as if they were the six legs of a terrified spider.
“I am running,” he gasped.

“But try and run like this,” the Carl admonished, and he gave a wriggling bound and a sudden outstretching and scurrying of shanks, and he disappeared from Cael’s sight in one wild spatter of big boots.

Despair fell on Cael of the Iron, but he had a great heart. “I will run until I burst,” he shrieked, “and when I burst, may I burst to a great distance, and may I trip that beggar-man up with my burstings and make him break his leg.”

He settled then to a determined, savage, implacable trot. He caught up on the Carl at last, for the latter had stopped to eat blackberries from the bushes on the road, and when he drew nigh, Cael began to jeer and sneer angrily at the Carl.
“Who lost the tails of his coat?” he roared.
“Don’t ask riddles of a man that’s eating blackberries,” the Carl rebuked him.
“The dog without a tall and the coat without a tail,” cried Cael.
“I give it up,” the Carl mumbled.
“It’s yourself, beggarman,” jeered Cael.
“I am myself,” the Carl gurgled through a mouthful of blackberries, “and as I am myself, how can it be myself? That is a silly riddle,” he burbled.
“Look at your coat, tub of grease?”
The Carl did so.

“My faith,” said he, “where are the two tails of my coat?” “I could smell one of them and it wrapped around a little tree thirty miles back,” said Cael, “and the other one was dishonouring a bush ten miles behind that.”

“It is bad luck to be separated from the tails of your own coat,” the Carl grumbled. “I’ll have to go back for them. Wait here, beloved, and eat blackberries until I come back, and we’ll both start fair.”
“Not half a second will I wait,” Cael replied, and he began to run towards Ben Edair as a lover runs to his maiden or as a bee flies to his hive.
“I haven’t had half my share of blackberries either,” the Carl lamented as he started to run backwards for his coat-tails.

He ran determinedly on that backward journey, and as the path he had travelled was beaten out as if it had been trampled by an hundred bulls yoked neck to neck, he was able to find the two bushes and the two coat-tails. He sewed them on his coat.

Then he sprang up, and he took to a fit and a vortex and an exasperation of running for which no description may be found. The thumping of his big boots grew as con-tinuous as the pattering of hailstones on a roof, and the wind of his passage blew trees down. The beasts that were ranging beside his path dropped dead from concussion, and the steam that snored from his nose blew birds into bits and made great lumps of cloud fall out of the sky.
He again caught up on Cael, who was running with his head down and his toes up.
“If you won’t try to run, my treasure,” said the Carl, “you will never get your tribute.”
And with that he incensed and exploded himself into an eye-blinding, continuous, waggle and complexity of boots that left Cael behind him in a flash.
“I will run until I burst,” sobbed Cael, and he screwed agitation and despair into his legs until he hummed and buzzed like a blue-bottle on a window.
Five miles from Ben Edair the Carl stopped, for he had again come among blackberries.

He ate of these until he was no more than a sack of juice, and when he heard the humming and buzzing of Cael of the Iron he mourned and lamented that he could not wait to eat his fill He took off his coat, stuffed it full of blackberries, swung it on his shoulders, and went bounding stoutly and nimbly for Ben Edair.
CHAPTER VI
It would be hard to tell of the terror that was in Fionn’s breast and in the hearts of the Fianna while they attended the conclusion of that race.
They discussed it unendingly, and at some moment of the day a man upbraided Fionn because he had not found Caelte the son of Rona’n as had been agreed on.
“There is no one can run like Caelte,” one man averred.
“He covers the ground,” said another.
“He is light as a feather.”
“Swift as a stag.” “Lunged like a bull.”
“Legged like a wolf.”
“He runs!”
These things were said to Fionn, and Fionn said these things to himself.
With every passing minute a drop of lead thumped down into every heart, and a pang of despair stabbed up to every brain.
“Go,” said Fionn to a hawk-eyed man, “go to the top of this hill and watch for the coming of the racers.”
And he sent lithe men with him so that they might run back in endless succession with the news.
The messengers began to run through his tent at minute intervals calling “nothing,” “nothing,” “nothing,” as they paused and darted away.
And the words, “nothing, nothing, nothing,” began to drowse into the brains of every person present.
“What can we hope from that Carl?” a champion demanded savagely.
“Nothing,” cried a messenger who stood and sped.
“A clump!” cried a champion.
“A hog!” said another.
“A flat-footed.”
“Little-wlnded.”
“Big-bellied.”
“Lazy-boned.”
“Pork!”
“Did you think, Fionn, that a whale could swim on land, or what did you imagine that lump could do?”
“Nothing,” cried a messenger, and was sped as he spoke.

Rage began to gnaw in Fionn’s soul, and a red haze danced and flickered before his eyes. His hands began to twitch and a desire crept over him to seize on champions by the neck, and to shake and worry and rage among them like a wild dog raging among sheep.
He looked on one, and yet he seemed to look on all at once.
“Be silent,” he growled. “Let each man be silent as a dead man.”

And he sat forward, seeing all, seeing none, with his mouth drooping open, and such a wildness and bristle lowering from that great glum brow that the champions shivered as though already in the chill of death, and were silent.
He rose and stalked to the tent-door.
“Where to, O Fionn?” said a champion humbly.
“To the hill-top,” said Fionn, and he stalked on.
They followed him, whispering among themselves, keeping their eyes on the ground as they climbed.
CHAPTER VII
“What do you see?” Fionn demanded of the watcher.
“Nothing,” that man replied.
“Look again,” said Fionn.
The eagle-eyed man lifted a face, thin and sharp as though it had been carven on the wind, and he stared forward with an immobile intentness.
“What do you see?” said Fionn.
“Nothing,” the man replied.
“I will look myself,” said Fionn, and his great brow bent forward and gloomed afar.
The watcher stood beside, staring with his tense face and unwinking, lidless eye.
“What can you see, O Fionn?” said the watcher.

“I can see nothing,” said Fionn, and he projected again his grim, gaunt forehead. For it seemed as if the watcher stared with his whole face, aye, and with his hands; but Fionn brooded weightedly on distance with his puckered and crannied brow.
They looked again.
“What can you see?” said Fionn.
“I see nothing,” said the watcher.
“I do not know if I see or if I surmise, but something moves,” said Fionn. “There is a trample,” he said.
The watcher became then an eye, a rigidity, an intense out-thrusting and ransacking of thin-spun distance. At last he spoke.
“There is a dust,” he said.
And at that the champions gazed also, straining hungrily afar, until their eyes became filled with a blue darkness and they could no longer see even the things that were close to them.
“I,” cried Cona’n triumphantly, “I see a dust.”
“And I,” cried another.
“And I.”
“I see a man,” said the eagle-eyed watcher.

And again they stared, until their straining eyes grew dim with tears and winks, and they saw trees that stood up and sat down, and fields that wobbled and spun round and round in a giddily swirling world.
“There is a man,” Cona’n roared.
“A man there is,” cried another.
“And he is carrying a man on his back,” said the watcher.
“It is Cael of the Iron carrying the Carl on his back,” he groaned.
“The great pork!” a man gritted.
“The no-good!” sobbed another.
“The lean-hearted.”
“Thick-thighed.”
“Ramshackle.”
“Muddle-headed.”
“Hog!” screamed a champion.
And he beat his fists angrily against a tree.
But the eagle-eyed watcher watched until his eyes narrowed and became pin-points, and he ceased to be a man and became an optic.
“Wait,” he breathed, “wait until I screw into one other inch of sight.”
And they waited, looking no longer on that scarcely perceptible speck in the distance, but straining upon the eye of the watcher as though they would penetrate it and look through it.
“It is the Carl,” he said, “carrying something on his back, and behind him again there is a dust.”
“Are you sure?” said Fionn in a voice that rumbled and vibrated like thunder.
“It is the Carl,” said the watcher, “and the dust behind him is Cael of the Iron trying to catch him up.”

Then the Fianna gave a roar of exultation, and each man seized his neighbour and kissed him on both cheeks; and they gripped hands about Fionn, and they danced round and round in a great circle, roaring with laughter and relief, in the ecstasy which only comes where grisly fear has been and whence that bony jowl has taken itself away.
CHAPTER VIII
The Carl of the Drab Coat came bumping and stumping and clumping into the camp, and was surrounded by a multitude that adored him and hailed him with tears.
“Meal!” he bawled, “meal for the love of the stars!”
And he bawled, “Meal, meal!” until he bawled everybody into silence.
Fionn addressed him.
“What for the meal, dear heart?”
“For the inside of my mouth,” said the Carl, “for the recesses and crannies and deep-down profundities of my stomach. Meal, meal!” he lamented.
Meal was brought.
The Carl put his coat on the ground, opened it carefully, and revealed a store of blackberries, squashed, crushed, mangled, democratic, ill-looking.
“The meal!” he groaned, “the meal!”
It was given to him.
“What of the race, my pulse?” said Fionn.
“Wait, wait,” cried the Carl. “I die, I die for meal and blackberries.”

Into the centre of the mess of blackberries he discharged a barrel of meal, and be mixed the two up and through, and round and down, until the pile of white-black, red-brown slibber-slobber reached up to his shoulders. Then he commenced to paw and impel and project and cram the mixture into his mouth, and between each mouthful he sighed a contented sigh, and during every mouthful he gurgled an oozy gurgle.

But while Fionn and the Fianna stared like lost minds upon the Carl, there came a sound of buzzing, as if a hornet or a queen of the wasps or a savage, steep-winged griffin was hovering about them, and looking away they saw Cael of the Iron charging on them with a monstrous extension and scurry of his legs. He had a sword in his hand, and there was nothing in his face but redness and ferocity.

Fear fell llke night around the Fianna, and they stood with slack knees and hanging hands waiting for death. But the Carl lifted a pawful of his oozy slop and discharged this at Cael with such a smash that the man’s head spun off his shoulders and hopped along the ground. The Carl then picked up the head and threw it at the body with such aim and force that the neck part of the head jammed into the neck part of the body and stuck there, as good a head as ever, you would have said, but that it bad got twisted the wrong way round. The Carl then lashed his opponent hand and foot.
“Now, dear heart, do you still claim tribute and lordship of Ireland?” said he.
“Let me go home,” groaned Cael, “I want to go home.”
“Swear by the sun and moon, if I let you go home, that you will send to Fionn, yearly and every year, the rent of the land of Thessaly.”
“I swear that,” said Cael, “and I would swear anything to get home.”

The Carl lifted him then and put him sitting into his ship. Then he raised his big boot and gave the boat a kick that drove it seven leagues out into the sea, and that was how the adventure of Cael of the Iron finished.
“Who are you, sir?” said Fionn to the Carl.
But before answering the Carl’s shape changed into one of splendour and delight.
“I am ruler of the Shi’ of Rath Cruachan,” he said.
Then Fionn mac Uail made a feast and a banquet for the jovial god, and with that the tale is ended of the King of Thessaly’s son and the Carl of the Drab Coat.

それだけでも驚くべきことだ。妖精の国へ行ったことや、その状態で身に起こったことを何か覚えている人は、ほとんどいないのだから。
実のところ、わたしたちは妖精の国へ行くのではなく、妖精の国になるのであり、脈のひと打ちのあいだに一年も千年も生きることがある。けれども戻ってくると記憶はたちまち曇り、たしかに妖精の国にいたのに、夢を見たか幻を見たかのように思えるのである。
だから、フィンがあの大きく引き延ばされた一瞬に身に起こったことをすべて覚えていたのは驚くべきことだったが、この話にはさらに驚くべきことがある。フィンが妖精の国へ行っただけでなく、彼がベン・エダール[ホウスの丘]に集めた大軍もまた運ばれていき、彼も彼らも、この世に戻ってくるまで、この世を離れたことに気づかなかったのである。

十四の軍団、予備のフィアナ七軍団と正規のフィアナ七軍団が、首領に率いられて大行軍と演習に出ていた。ベン・エダールに着くと、フィンが翌日のために思い描いていた戦の計画に備えて兵を休ませるため、野営することに決まった。野営地が選ばれ、軍勢の各部隊と各中隊はそれぞれふさわしい場所に宿営したので、混み合うこともなく、行軍が止まったり途切れたりすることもなかった。中隊が止まったところがその休み場所で、そこでは他の中隊の邪魔にならず、自分たちもくつろげたのである。
これが済むと、大隊の指揮官たちは海を見下ろす平らな草地の台地に集まり、翌日の演習について協議が始まった。その話し合いのあいだ、彼らは眼下にしわを寄せきらめいて広がる大海原をたびたび眺めた。
帆をいっぱいに張った広々とした船が一艘、東からベン・エダールめざして進んでいた。
話し合いが途切れるたびに、ときおり勇士の一人が目をやって、急ぐその船のことを口にした。フィンとフィアナにこの冒険が起こったのは、そうした一瞬のことだったのかもしれない。
「あの船はどこから来たのだろう」とコナンが何気なく言った。
けれども、それが戦の備えのよく整った船だということのほかは、だれにも何もわからなかった。
船が岸に寄ってくると、見ていた者たちは、背の高い男が槍の柄を使って舷側からひらりと跳び降りるのを見た。まもなくこの紳士の来訪がフィンに告げられ、御前へ連れてこられた。
まことに頑丈で好戦的で、ずけずけとした人物であった。驚くほど堅固な鎧に身を固め、頭には彫刻を施した硬い兜をかぶり、肩には赤い浮き彫りのついた見事な盾を揺らし、腿のあたりには幅広い溝のあるまっすぐな剣をがちゃつかせていた。盾の下の肩には見事な緋色のマントをまとい、胸には焼き金の大きなブローチをつけ、拳には柄の太い、磨いていない槍を二本握っていた。
フィンと勇士たちはこの紳士を見て、その物腰と装備にたいそう感心した。
「若い方、どの血筋の者か」とフィンは問いただした。「そして世界の四隅のどこから来たのか」
「わが名は鉄のカイル」と見知らぬ男は答えた。「テッサリア王の息子だ」
「どんな用向きでここへ来たのか」
「わしは用向きで出歩きはせぬ」と男は厳しく答えた。「気の向く事柄のために出歩くのだ」
「それならそれでよい。この国へそなたを連れてきた気の向く事柄とは何か」
「国を出てこのかた、わしはどの国からもどの島からも、それがわしに貢ぎを納め、わしを主と認めるまでは去ったことがない」
「それでこの国へ来たというのか」とフィンは耳を疑って叫んだ。
「貢ぎと主権のためにな」と相手はうなり、槍の柄を激しく地面に打ちつけた。
「わが手にかけて」とコナンが言った。「どれほど偉大な戦士であろうと、アイルランドにその好敵手が見つからなかった者の話など聞いたことがない。そういう者たちの弔いの歌は、みなこの国の女たちに歌われてきたのだ」
「わが手と言葉にかけて」と荒々しい見知らぬ男は言った。「お前の話を聞いていると、小僧か愚か者を思い出す」
「気をつけられよ」とフィンは言った。「ゲールの勇士と大竜たちがそなたのそばに立ち、我らのまわりにはアイルランドのフィアナの十四軍団がいるのだ」
「この七年に死んだフィアナをみな、今ここにいる者たちに加えたとしても」と見知らぬ男は言い放った。「わしはそいつらもこいつらもひどい目に遭わせ、手足と命を切り縮めてやる」
「小さな大言ではないな」とコナンは男を見つめてつぶやいた。
「大言などではない」とカイルは言った。「わしの力量と格を示すために、一つの勝負を持ちかけよう」
「その勝負を言ってみよ」とフィンは命じた。
「こうだ」とカイルは冷ややかな猛々しさで言った。「お前の十四の大隊のなかに、わしより速く走るか、わしを組み伏せるか、わしを打ち負かす男が見つかれば、わしは自分の国へ引き上げ、二度とお前たちを煩わせぬ」
その口調はあまりに荒々しく、睨みつける目はあまりに挑戦的だったので、勇士たちは狼狽にとらわれはじめ、フィンでさえ息が止まったような気がした。
「英雄らしい言葉だ」と少しして彼は認めた。「その条件でそなたの相手が見つからないとしても、名乗り出る者が足りないためではあるまい」
「走ることだけなら」とフィンは考え深げに続けた。「我らには名高い勇士、キールタ・マク・ローナンがいる」
「そのローナンの息子も、長くは名高くあるまい」と見知らぬ男は言い放った。
「あいつは赤鹿を追い抜く」とコナンが言った。
「風よりも速く走る」とフィンが叫んだ。
「赤鹿や風を追い抜けとは言われまい」と見知らぬ男はあざ笑った。「わしを追い抜けと言われるのだ」と雷のように言った。「その走り手を連れてこい。お前たちに思わせたほど、そいつの足に大きな度胸が宿っているかどうか、確かめてやろう」
「あいつはここにいないのだ」とコナンが嘆いた。
「そういう名高い戦士は、呼び出しがかかったとき決してその場にいないものだ」と厳めしい見知らぬ男は言った。
「わが手にかけて」とフィンは叫んだ。「あいつはほどなくここに来る。わし自ら迎えに行くのだから」
「それならそれでよい」とカイルは言った。「そしてわしの留守のあいだ」とフィンは続けた。「約束として言い置く。そなたはここにいるフィアナと友誼を結び、友誼のあらゆる条件と礼を守ること」
カイルはそれに同意した。
「お前が戻るまで、この者たちのだれも傷つけはせぬ」と彼は言った。
それからフィンは王たちのタラへ向けて出発した。キールタ・マク・ローナンはきっとそこにいるだろうと思ったからである。「もしそこにいなければ」と勇士は独りごちた。「フィアナのケシュ・コランで見つかるだろう」
第二章
ベン・エダールからさほど遠くへ行かないうちに、フィンは入り組んだ薄暗い森に来た。木々があまりに密に生い茂り、下生えがあまりにはびこり絡み合っていて、ほとんど通り抜けられないほどだった。かつて森を切り開いて道が通されたことを思い出して、彼はそれを探した。それは深くえぐれた窪んだ道で、森の端から端までまっすぐに、あるいはのたうつように続いていた。

この薄暗い溝へフィンは下りて進んでいったが、湿った森の奥深くまで入り込んだとき、どすんどすん、ぐしゃぐしゃという足音が聞こえ、恐ろしい、邪悪な顔つきの者がこちらへやって来るのが見えた。荒々しく途方もなく大きな、黄色い肌で骨太の巨人で、身につけているのは、仕立ての悪い、泥のこびりついたくすんだ色の外套だけだった。その外套は大きな裸のふくらはぎにぶらぶら揺れてぱたぱたと当たっていた。踏み鳴らす足には、舟の形をしていながら舟より大きい、どでかい革靴を履いていて、足を下ろすたびに、窪んだ道から樽いっぱいの泥をぐしゃりと押しつぶして噴き出させた。
フィンはこれほど巨大な人物を見たことがなく、立ちつくして驚きのあまり見つめていた。
大男は彼に挨拶した。
「たった一人かね、フィン」と大男は叫んだ。「どうしてフィアナの戦士が一人も隊長のそばにいないのかね」この問いにフィンは我に返った。
「それは話すには長すぎる話で、込み入っていて急を要するし、それに今は割く暇もないのだ」
「それでも今話しなさいよ」と化け物じみた男は言い張った。
そう迫られて、フィンは鉄のカイルがやって来たこと、カイルが出した挑戦のこと、そして自分フィンがキールタ・マク・ローナンを探しに王たちのタラへ向かっていることを話した。
「その異国の男ならよく知っている」と大男は言った。
「あいつは自分で言うほどの勇士なのか」とフィンは尋ねた。
「自分でやると言った倍のことができるさ」と化け物は答えた。
「キールタ・マク・ローナンより速くは走るまい」とフィンは言い張った。大男はあざ笑った。
「ハリネズミより速く走るまい、とでも言っておきなさいよ、あんた。お前さんのキールタがそろそろ出ようかと思いはじめるころには、そのカイルは走り終えているよ」
「それでは」とフィンは言った。「どこへ向かえばよいのか、どうすればアイルランドの名誉を守れるのか、もうわからない」
「わしはそういうことのやり方を知っている」と相手はゆっくりうなずいて言った。
「知っているなら」とフィンは懇願した。「名誉にかけてわしに教えてくれ」
「そうしよう」と男は答えた。
「膝の錆びついた、のろのろ走りのローナンの息子など、もう探しなさんな」と男は続けた。「わしにお前さんの競走を走ってくれと頼みなさい。そうすれば、この手にかけて、わしが一番に決勝の杭に着いてみせる」
これを聞いて首領は笑いだした。
「わが良き友よ、お前さんは外套の裾それぞれにこびりついた二トンの泥を運ぶだけで手いっぱいだろう。その重い靴は言うに及ばずだ」
「この手にかけて」と男は叫んだ。「アイルランドでその競走に勝てるのはわしのほかにだれもいない。わしにやらせてくれ」
それでフィンは承知した。「それならそれでよい」と彼は言った。「では、名を教えてくれ」
「わしはくすんだ外套の無骨者と呼ばれている」
「名はどれも名だ」とフィンは応じた。「それもまた一つの名だ」
それから二人はベン・エダールへ戻った。
第三章
二人が軍勢のなかに来ると、アイルランドの男たちは巨大な見知らぬ男のまわりに集まった。笑っているのを見られないようにマントに顔を埋める者もいれば、面白がって地面を転げ回る者もいた。また、口をぽかんと開け、膝を曲げ、腕をだらりと垂らして、すっかり呆然としたかのように、ただ見知らぬ男を唖然と見つめることしかできない者もいた。
鉄のカイルもその場にやって来て、見知らぬ男を細かく念入りに調べた。
「悪魔の名にかけて、こいつはいったい何だ」と彼はフィンに尋ねた。
「なあ、あんた」とフィンは言った。「これが競走でそなたに当てる勇士だ」
鉄のカイルは顔を紫色にし、怒りのあまり舌を呑み込みそうになった。
「永遠の終わりまで」と彼は吼えた。「最後の審判のまさに最後の瞬間まで、この脂じみた、でか蹄の、つぎはぎだらけの乞食もどきと競走するのに、片足たりとも動かすものか」
けれどもこれを聞いて無骨者は大笑いを爆発させたので、その場にいる戦士たちの鼓膜は頭のなかで破れそうになった。
「安心しなさいよ、いとしい人、わしは乞食じゃない。わしの素性は、この集まりのなかでいちばん上品な王子の血より卑しくはないさ。そんなふうに挑戦から逃げられやしないよ、あんた。わしと一緒に走るか、わしに追われて船まで走るか、どっちかだ。どれくらいの距離を走るつもりかね、あんた」
「わしは六十マイルより短く走ったことはない」とカイルはむっつりと答えた。
「短い距離だが」と無骨者は言った。「まあいいだろう。ここからマンスターの藺草の丘、スリーヴ・ルアクラまでがちょうど六十マイルだ。それでいいかね」
「どうやろうとかまわん」とカイルは答えた。
「それなら」と無骨者は言った。「今からスリーヴ・ルアクラへ行って、朝になったらそこからここまで競走を始めよう」
「そのようにしよう」とカイルは言った。
そこで二人はマンスターへ向けて出発し、日が沈むころスリーヴ・ルアクラに着いて、そこで夜を過ごす支度をした。
第四章
「カイル、わが脈よ」と無骨者は言った。「夜を過ごすのに、家か小屋を建てたほうがいい」
「わしは何も建てんぞ」とカイルは、ひどく不快そうに無骨者を見て答えた。
「建てない、だと」
「ここで一晩過ごすためだけに家も小屋も建てはせん。こんな場所は二度と見たくないからな」
「それなら家はわしが自分で建てよう」と無骨者は言った。「建てるのを手伝わない者は、家の外にいればいい」
無骨者は近くの森へどすどすと歩いていき、二十四対の大きな材木を切り倒して結び合わせるまで休まなかった。それを片方の脇に抱え込み、もう片方の脇には寝床にする藺草の束をはさんで、そのひと荷だけで、しっかり屋根を葺いた居心地のよい家を大急ぎで建て上げ、余った材木で家の床に焚き火をこしらえた。
連れの男は離れたところに座って、怒りと嫌悪を浮かべてその仕事を眺めていた。
「さあカイル、いとしい人」と無骨者は言った。「男なら、食べるものを探すのを手伝ってくれ。ここには獲物がいるから」
「自分でやれ」とカイルは吼えた。「わしの望みは、お前のそばにいないことだけだ」
「手伝わない歯には、分け前もない」と相手は答えた。
まもなく無骨者は、走って追いつめた野猪を一頭持って戻ってきた。焚き火でその獣を焼いて半分を食べ、残りの半分は朝食に取っておいた。それから藺草の上に横になり、二度寝返りを打つと眠り込んだ。
けれどもカイルは丘の斜面に野宿し、その夜眠ったとしても、腹をすかせたまま眠ったのだった。それでも朝、無骨者を起こしたのは彼だった。
「起きろ、乞食、わしと競走するつもりならな」
無骨者は目をこすった。
「わしは眠り足りるまで決して起きないし、まだあと一時間は眠っていいはずだ。けれど急いでいるなら、いとしい人、今すぐ走りだしなさい、祝福を送るよ。わしは目が覚めたら、お前さんの足跡をとことこ追いかけるから」
そこでカイルは走りはじめた。先に出られるのはありがたかった。相手があまりに自分を相手にしていないので、無骨者が走りだしたら何が起こるのか見当もつかなかったからである。
「それでも」とカイルは独りごちた。「一時間も先に出れば、あの乞食がわしに追いつくには骨を折らねばなるまい」そして彼は腰を据えて、ばたばたと力強く走りだした。
第五章
一時間たって無骨者は目を覚ました。猪の残り半分を食べ、しゃぶっていない骨を外套の裾に結びつけた。それから猪の骨をがらがらと大きく鳴らしながら出発した。
彼がどのように、どれほどの速さで走ったかを語るのは難しい。けれども彼は二本足で大きく跳びながら進み、ときには一本足で泥をはね散らす途方もない跳躍で進み、またときには、大きく広げ、遠くへ投げ出し、恐ろしく踏み鳴らし、空間を打ち砕くような脚で走った。
燕を眠っているかのように置き去りにした。赤鹿に追いつくと跳び越えて、立ち止まらせたままにした。風はいつも彼の後ろにあった。そのたびに風を追い抜いたからである。そして跳んだり弾んだりしながら鉄のカイルに追いついた。カイルはよく走っていて、拳を上げ、頭をそらし、二本の脚をあまりに激しく出し入れしていたので、その速い動きのせいで脚が見えないほどだったのだが。
カイルのそばをとことこ走りながら、無骨者は外套の裾に手を突っ込み、赤い骨をひとつかみ引っぱり出した。
「ほら、あんた、肉のついた骨だ」と彼は言った。「かわいそうに、ひと晩じゅう何も食べていないんだから、骨から少しかじれば、お腹が落ち着くよ」
「汚いものはしまっておけ、乞食」と相手は答えた。「お前がしゃぶった骨をかじるくらいなら、首を吊られたほうがましだ」
「どうして走らないんだい、わが脈よ」と無骨者は真顔で言った。「どうして競走に勝とうとしないんだい」
そこでカイルは、手足をまるで蠅の羽のように、小魚のひれのように、あるいは怯えた蜘蛛の六本の脚のように動かしはじめた。
「走っているとも」と彼はあえいだ。
「でも、こんなふうに走ってごらん」と無骨者はたしなめ、身をくねらせてひと跳びし、急に脛を伸ばしてせかせかと動かすと、大きな靴の荒々しいはねの一撃とともにカイルの視界から消えてしまった。
鉄のカイルは絶望に襲われたが、彼には大きな度胸があった。「破裂するまで走ってやる」と彼は金切り声をあげた。「そして破裂するときは、遠くまで破裂して、その破片であの乞食をつまずかせ、脚を折らせてやる」
それから彼は、決然として、猛々しく、容赦のない小走りに腰を据えた。とうとう彼は無骨者に追いついた。無骨者は道ばたの茂みのブラックベリーを食べようと立ち止まっていたのである。近づくとカイルは、腹立たしげに無骨者をあざけり、からかいはじめた。
「外套の裾をなくしたのはだれだ」と彼は吼えた。
「ブラックベリーを食べている男になぞなぞを出すもんじゃない」と無骨者はたしなめた。
「尻尾のない犬と、裾のない外套」とカイルは叫んだ。
「降参だ」と無骨者はもごもご言った。
「お前のことだよ、乞食」とカイルはあざけった。
「わしはわしだ」と無骨者はブラックベリーを口いっぱいに頬張ったまま、ごぼごぼと言った。「わしがわしなのに、どうしてそれがわしなんだ。くだらないなぞなぞだ」と彼はぶつぶつ言った。
「自分の外套を見てみろ、脂の樽め」
無骨者はそうした。
「おやまあ」と彼は言った。「わしの外套の二つの裾はどこへ行った」「一つは三十マイル後ろで小さな木に巻きついていて、においでわかったぞ」とカイルは言った。「もう一つは、そのさらに十マイル後ろで茂みを汚していた」
「自分の外套の裾と離れ離れになるのは縁起が悪い」と無骨者はぼやいた。「取りに戻らなきゃならん。ここで待っていてくれ、いとしい人、わしが戻るまでブラックベリーを食べていなさい。そうしたら二人とも公平に出発しよう」
「半秒たりとも待つものか」とカイルは答え、恋人が乙女のもとへ走るように、蜂が巣へ飛ぶように、ベン・エダールへ向かって走りだした。
「わしもブラックベリーの分け前を半分も食べていないのに」と無骨者は、外套の裾を取りに後ろ向きに走りだしながら嘆いた。
彼はその戻り道を決然と走った。自分の通ってきた道は、首と首をつながれた百頭の雄牛に踏み荒らされたように踏み固められていたので、二つの茂みと二つの外套の裾を見つけることができた。彼はそれを外套に縫いつけた。
それから跳び上がり、どんな描写も見つからないような、発作と渦巻きと激昂の走りにとりかかった。大きな靴の踏み鳴らす音は、屋根を打つ雹のぱらぱらという音のように絶え間なくなり、通り過ぎる風が木々を吹き倒した。道のそばをうろついていた獣たちは衝撃で倒れ死に、鼻から鼾のように噴き出す湯気は鳥を粉々に吹き飛ばし、空から大きな雲の塊を落とした。
彼はふたたびカイルに追いついた。カイルは頭を下げ、爪先を上げて走っていた。
「走ろうとしないなら、わが宝よ」と無骨者は言った。「貢ぎは決して手に入らないよ」
そう言うと彼は、自らを燃え立たせ爆発させて、目もくらむばかりの、絶え間ない、靴の揺れと入り乱れとなり、たちまちカイルを後ろに置き去りにした。
「破裂するまで走ってやる」とカイルはすすり泣き、脚に焦りと絶望をねじ込んだので、窓にとまった青蠅のようにぶんぶん唸った。
ベン・エダールまで五マイルのところで無骨者は立ち止まった。またブラックベリーの茂みに来たからである。
彼はそれを食べて、ついには果汁の詰まった袋にすぎなくなった。そして鉄のカイルのぶんぶんという唸りが聞こえてくると、腹いっぱい食べるまで待てないのを悲しみ嘆いた。外套を脱いでブラックベリーをいっぱいに詰め込み、肩にかつぐと、たくましく身軽にベン・エダールへ跳ねていった。
第六章
その競走の決着を待つあいだ、フィンの胸とフィアナの心にどれほどの恐怖があったかを語るのは難しい。
彼らは果てしなくそのことを論じ合い、その日のある時、一人の男が、取り決めどおりにローナンの息子キールタを見つけてこなかったとフィンを責めた。
「キールタほど走れる者はいない」と一人の男が言い張った。
「あいつは大地を駆け抜ける」と別の男が言った。
「羽のように軽い」
「牡鹿のように速い」「雄牛のような肺だ」
「狼のような脚だ」
「あいつは走るぞ」
こうしたことがフィンに向かって言われ、フィンもこうしたことを自分に言い聞かせた。
一分過ぎるごとに、どの心にも鉛のしずくがどすんと落ち、どの頭にも絶望の痛みが突き上げた。
「行け」とフィンは鷹の目を持つ男に言った。「この丘の頂へ行って、走者たちが来るのを見張れ」
そして、次から次へと途切れなく知らせを持って走って戻れるよう、身軽な男たちを彼につけてやった。
使いの者たちは一分おきに彼の天幕を駆け抜けはじめ、立ち止まってはさっと去りながら「何もない」「何もない」「何もない」と叫んだ。
そして「何もない、何もない、何もない」という言葉が、その場にいるすべての者の頭のなかでまどろむように響きはじめた。
「あの無骨者に何を期待できるというのだ」と一人の勇士が荒々しく問いただした。
「何もない」と、立ち止まってはまた駆け出す使いの者が叫んだ。
「でくの坊め」と一人の勇士が叫んだ。
「豚め」と別の者が言った。
「べた足め」
「息切れ野郎」
「太鼓腹」
「怠け骨」
「豚肉め」
「フィンよ、鯨が陸を泳げるとでも思ったのか。あの塊に何ができると思ったのだ」
「何もない」と使いの者が叫び、言うそばから駆け去った。
フィンの魂には怒りが噛みつきはじめ、目の前には赤い靄が踊りちらついた。手はぴくぴく動きはじめ、勇士たちの首をつかんで揺さぶり、羊の群れのなかで荒れ狂う野犬のように彼らのなかで噛みつき荒れ狂いたいという欲望が忍び寄ってきた。
彼は一人を見たが、それでいて同時に全員を見ているようだった。
「黙れ」と彼はうなった。「一人残らず、死人のように黙っていろ」
そして彼は身を乗り出して座り、すべてを見ていながら何も見ず、口をだらりと開けていた。その大きな陰鬱な額からはあまりの荒々しさと逆立つ気配が垂れこめていたので、勇士たちはすでに死の冷気のなかにいるかのように身震いし、黙りこんだ。
彼は立ち上がり、天幕の戸口へ大股に歩いていった。
「どちらへ、おおフィンよ」と一人の勇士がへりくだって言った。
「丘の頂へだ」とフィンは言い、大股に歩き続けた。
彼らはひそひそささやき合いながら、登るあいだ地面に目を落としてあとについていった。
第七章
「何が見える」とフィンは見張りに問いただした。
「何も」とその男は答えた。
「もう一度見よ」とフィンは言った。
鷲の目を持つ男は、風に彫り刻まれたかのように細く鋭い顔を上げ、微動だにせぬひたむきさで前方を見つめた。
「何が見える」とフィンは言った。
「何も」と男は答えた。
「わし自ら見よう」とフィンは言い、その大きな額を前へ傾けて、陰鬱に遠くを睨んだ。
見張りは張りつめた顔で、まばたきもせず、瞼のないような目で見つめながら、かたわらに立っていた。
「何が見えますか、おおフィンよ」と見張りは言った。
「何も見えぬ」とフィンは言い、ふたたびその厳めしく骨ばった額を突き出した。見張りは顔じゅうで、いや手でさえも見つめているように思われたが、フィンはしわの寄ったひび割れた額で、重々しく遠方に思いを凝らしていたからである。
二人はまた見つめた。
「何が見える」とフィンは言った。
「何も見えません」と見張りは言った。
「見えているのか推し量っているのかわからぬが、何かが動いている」とフィンは言った。「足音がする」と彼は言った。
そこで見張りは、一つの目となり、硬直となり、細く紡がれた遠方への激しい突出と探索となった。とうとう彼は口を開いた。
「土煙が立っています」と彼は言った。
それを聞いて勇士たちも目を凝らし、飢えたように遠くを見つめたので、とうとう目が青い闇でいっぱいになり、すぐ近くのものさえ見えなくなった。
「わしだ」とコナンが勝ち誇って叫んだ。「わしにも土煙が見える」
「わしにも」と別の者が叫んだ。
「わしにも」
「人が見えます」と鷲の目の見張りが言った。
そしてまた彼らは目を凝らし、ついには凝らした目が涙とまばたきでかすみ、立ち上がっては座る木々や、ぐらぐら揺れて目の回るように渦巻く世界でくるくる回る野原が見えるほどになった。
「人がいるぞ」とコナンが吼えた。
「人がいる」と別の者が叫んだ。
「そして人を背負っています」と見張りが言った。
「鉄のカイルが無骨者を背負っているのです」と彼はうめいた。
「あの大豚め」と一人の男が歯ぎしりした。
「役立たずめ」と別の者がすすり泣いた。
「腰抜け」
「太腿」
「がたがた野郎」
「とんま頭」
「豚め」と一人の勇士が金切り声をあげた。
そして彼は怒って木を拳で叩いた。
けれども鷲の目の見張りは、目が細まって針の先ほどになるまで見張り続け、人であることをやめて一つの視覚となった。
「待て」と彼はささやいた。「もう一インチ視界をねじ込むまで待ってくれ」
そこで彼らは待った。遠くのほとんど見分けられない点を見るのはやめ、まるで見張りの目を突き抜けてその向こうを見ようとするかのように、見張りの目に目を凝らした。
「無骨者です」と彼は言った。「何かを背負っていて、その後ろにまた土煙が立っています」
「確かか」とフィンは、雷のように轟き震える声で言った。
「無骨者です」と見張りは言った。「そして後ろの土煙は、追いつこうとしている鉄のカイルです」
そこでフィアナは歓喜の雄叫びをあげ、だれもが隣の者をつかまえて両頬に口づけした。彼らはフィンを囲んで手をつなぎ、大きな輪になってぐるぐると踊り、笑いと安堵に吼えた。それは、恐ろしい恐怖がそこにあって、その骨ばった顎が去っていったところにだけ訪れる恍惚であった。
第八章
くすんだ外套の無骨者は、どすんどすん、どしどし、どかどかと陣営に入ってきて、彼を崇め、涙で迎える大群衆に取り囲まれた。
「粉だ」と彼はわめいた。「星々の愛にかけて、粉をくれ」
そして「粉だ、粉だ」とわめき続けて、とうとうみなをわめき黙らせた。
フィンが彼に話しかけた。
「粉を何にするのだ、あんた」
「わしの口のなかのためさ」と無骨者は言った。「わしの胃袋の奥まった隅々と、深い深い底のためだ。粉だ、粉だ」と彼は嘆いた。
粉が運ばれてきた。
無骨者は外套を地面に置いて注意深く広げ、つぶれ、ひしゃげ、ぐちゃぐちゃで、ありふれた、見栄えの悪いブラックベリーの蓄えを見せた。
「粉を」と彼はうめいた。「粉を」
粉が彼に与えられた。
「競走はどうなったのだ、わが脈よ」とフィンは言った。
「待ってくれ、待ってくれ」と無骨者は叫んだ。「わしは死ぬ、粉とブラックベリーが欲しくて死にそうだ」
ブラックベリーの山の真ん中に、彼は樽一杯の粉をぶちまけ、その二つを混ぜに混ぜ、上へ下へ、ぐるぐると、白黒で赤茶色のどろどろの山が肩に届くほどになるまでかき混ぜた。それから彼はその混ぜ物を手でかき、押しやり、放り込み、口に詰め込みはじめた。ひと口ごとに満足のため息をつき、ひと口頬張るたびにぐちゅぐちゅと喉を鳴らした。
けれども、フィンとフィアナが正気を失った者のように無骨者を見つめているあいだに、まるで雀蜂か女王蜂か、切り立った翼の獰猛なグリフィンがまわりを舞っているかのような、ぶんぶんという音が聞こえてきた。目をやると、鉄のカイルが途方もなく脚を伸ばしせかせかと動かして、彼らめがけて突進してくるのが見えた。手には剣を持ち、その顔には赤さと獰猛さしかなかった。

恐怖が夜のようにフィアナのまわりに降り、彼らは膝の力が抜け、手をだらりと垂らして、死を待って立ちつくした。けれども無骨者はどろどろの混ぜ物をひとつかみ持ち上げ、カイルめがけてあまりの勢いで投げつけたので、男の首は肩からくるりと飛んで、地面をぴょんぴょん跳ねていった。それから無骨者はその首を拾い上げ、狙いすまして力いっぱい胴体へ投げつけたので、首の付け根が胴体の首の部分にはまり込んでくっつき、これまでと同じくらい立派な首だと言いたくなるほどだった。ただ、後ろ前にねじれてしまっていたが。それから無骨者は相手の手足を縛り上げた。
「さて、あんた、まだアイルランドの貢ぎと主権を求めるかね」と彼は言った。
「家に帰らせてくれ」とカイルはうめいた。「家に帰りたい」
「家に帰らせてやったら、毎年毎年テッサリアの地代をフィンに送ると、太陽と月にかけて誓え」
「誓う」とカイルは言った。「家に帰れるなら何でも誓う」
そこで無骨者は彼を持ち上げて船に座らせた。それから大きな靴を上げて船をひと蹴りすると、船は沖へ七リーグも飛んでいった。こうして鉄のカイルの冒険は終わったのである。
「あなたはどなたですか」とフィンは無骨者に言った。
けれども答える前に、無骨者の姿は輝きと喜びに満ちた姿に変わった。
「わしはラス・クルアハンのシーの主だ」と彼は言った。
それからウァルの息子フィンは、この陽気な神のために祝宴と饗宴を催した。こうして、テッサリア王の息子とくすんだ外套の無骨者の話は終わる。
